why: Here Israel is the northern kingdom and its people ("the house of Israel"), not the patriarch Israel (Jacob).

In 2:22 'Jezreel' is the child's symbolic name ('God sows') standing for the people God will plant again, so it does not point to the child as a person here. The place Jezreel stays linked, since some readers also hear the fertile valley in it.

Here 'Israelites' means the people, not the patriarch. In 3:5 'David their king' is read by many Jews and Christians as the Davidic line or a coming king from it, and by others as David himself; the chapter's notes treat that, so the link is not made.

Here Israel and Ephraim mean the northern kingdom, not the patriarchs. Bible Atlas puts this Gilgal in the coastal plain, but the Gilgal Hosea warns against (4:15) was a sanctuary in the northern kingdom, so no dot is drawn.

Ephraim is the northern kingdom and 'Benjamin' in 5:8 is the tribe and its territory, not the patriarchs. The text names no Assyrian king here, so Tiglath-pileser is not linked. Bible Atlas puts Mizpah in Gilead, but the Mizpah of 5:1 may be Mizpah of Benjamin or another site, so no dot is drawn.
Here Ephraim is the northern kingdom, or its leading tribe, and not the patriarch Ephraim, son of Joseph.

Ephraim is the northern kingdom, not the patriarch. The 'Baal of Peor' in 9:10 is linked as the place Baal-peor, which recalls the worship at Peor in Numbers 25. Bible Atlas puts this Gilgal in the coastal plain, but Hosea's Gilgal (9:15) was a sanctuary in the northern kingdom, so no dot is drawn.

Ephraim and Israel mean the northern kingdom, not the patriarchs. No Assyrian king is named in 10:6 (the king there is called Jareb). 'Shalman' in 10:14 is of uncertain identity, and scholars differ on whether it is Shalmaneser V or another ruler, so no link is made.
Here Ephraim is the northern kingdom, or its leading tribe, and not the patriarch Ephraim, son of Joseph.

Ephraim is the northern kingdom. In 12:2-4 and 12:12 Jacob and Israel are the patriarch, so Jacob is linked and Israel kept. Bible Atlas puts this Gilgal in the coastal plain, but Hosea's Gilgal (12:11) was a sanctuary in the northern kingdom, so no dot is drawn. Bible Atlas's Aram is a point in Syria, but 12:12 means the region of Paddan-aram in upper Mesopotamia where Jacob fled, so no dot is drawn.
